title: YOUR SPOUSE IS NOT A SEXUAL OBJECT
paragraphs:
YOUR SPOUSE IS NOT A SEXUAL OBJECT
Reading 1 Corinthians 7 Without Weaponizing It — Because a Bible Verse Was Never Meant to Become a Weapon in the Bedroom
There is a particular kind of pain that happens when the person who promised to love you reaches for Scripture…and you realize they are not reaching for it to become more like Jesus.
They are reaching for it to win.
Maybe you have heard the verse.
Maybe you have quoted it.
Maybe someone quoted it while you were exhausted, grieving, sick, emotionally wounded, frightened, disconnected, or simply struggling.
“The wife hath not power of her own body, but the husband…”
And suddenly the Bible was no longer being opened like bread.
It was being held like a weapon.
But keep reading.
Please.
Because the sentence does not stop where some people have conveniently stopped it.
Paul continues:
“…and likewise also the husband hath not power of his own body, but the wife.”
That changes everything.

And if we are going to talk about sex, marriage, desire, obligation, rejection, intimacy, selfishness, manipulation, tenderness, and what husbands and wives owe one another, then we need enough courage to let Paul finish his sentence.
Because 1 Corinthians 7 does not hand one spouse ownership papers over the other.
Paul does something much more radical.
He dismantles selfishness on both sides.
The New Testament was written primarily in Koine Greek, so 1 Corinthians 7 is not a passage where Hebrew or Aramaic gives us the original wording. Greek does.
And the Greek matters.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 7:3:
In straightforward English:
Let the husband give to the wife what is due to her, and likewise the wife to the husband.
Notice the movement.
Husband toward wife.
Wife toward husband.
Not domination.
Reciprocity.
Not “What can I demand?”
But “What should I give?”
Paul then says something astonishing:
“ἡ γυνὴ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει…”
The wife does not exercise authority over her own body…
Someone determined to control a woman could stop reading right there.
But Paul does not.
“…ἀλλὰ ὁ ἀνήρ· ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει, ἀλλὰ ἡ γυνή.”
But the husband does; and likewise the husband does not exercise authority over his own body, but the wife does.
There it is again.
ὁμοίως — homoíōs.
Likewise.
Similarly.
In the same manner.
Paul refuses to give one spouse a principle he does not immediately apply reciprocally to the other.
That little word destroys a great deal of selfish theology.

If a husband reads verse 4 and hears, “Her body belongs to me, therefore I can demand whatever I want,” he has somehow managed to read the first half of Paul's argument while ignoring the second half that places his own body under the same reciprocal marital obligation.
And if either spouse reads the passage merely as ammunition for getting what he or she wants, something deeper has already gone wrong.
Because the controlling question of Christian marriage cannot simply be:
“What am I entitled to receive?”
Jesus keeps turning that question around:
“How can I love?”
“How can I serve?”
“How can I lay myself down?”
“How can I seek the good of the person God entrusted to my care?”
This is why 1 Corinthians 7 cannot be isolated from the rest of the New Testament.
The same apostolic witness that speaks about marital intimacy tells husbands:
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.” — Ephesians 5:25
Christ does not give husbands a model of predatory entitlement.
He gives them a cross.
Christ loved His bride by giving Himself.
Sacrificially.
Tenderly.
At terrible cost to Himself.
Peter likewise commands husbands to live with their wives “according to knowledge,” giving honor to them as fellow heirs of the grace of life (1 Peter 3:7).
And Paul describes love in words that should haunt every Christian who has ever used Scripture selfishly:
Love “seeketh not her own.” — 1 Corinthians 13:5
Read that again before demanding anything from your spouse.
Love does not insist upon its own way.
Christian marriage therefore cannot be reduced to two people standing across the bedroom keeping score.
“I did this for you.”
“You owe me that.”
“You rejected me yesterday.”
“You have to because we are married.”
“That is your duty.”
No.
Something sacred dies when intimacy becomes a debt-collection agency.
And something equally dangerous happens when affection and intimacy are deliberately weaponized as punishment, manipulation, revenge, or control.
Paul confronts that too.
He writes:
Do not deprive one another.
But once again, keep reading.
Paul immediately speaks about a temporary period of abstinence:
“εἰ μήτι ἂν ἐκ συμφώνου πρὸς καιρόν…”
except perhaps by agreement for a time.
That phrase matters enormously:
ἐκ συμφώνου — ek symphōnou.
By agreement.
By mutual accord.

The English word “consent” is often used in modern discussions, and we should be careful not to pretend Paul was writing a twenty-first-century legal or psychological definition of sexual consent. He was not.
But we should be equally careful not to erase what Paul actually did write.
When he discusses a temporary abstention from marital relations, he explicitly describes it as something undertaken together — by agreement.
Neither spouse is pictured as a disposable object.
Neither spouse is given permission to cultivate selfishness.
Neither spouse is told, “Your desires are the only desires that matter.”
The passage assumes a marriage in which husband and wife have obligations toward one another, and it expresses those obligations with striking reciprocity.
That is radically different from turning the passage into:
“You owe me your body whenever I demand it.”
A covenant is not a license for cruelty.
Marriage does not erase personhood.
And sexual intimacy is not biblical simply because it happens between married people.
The character of Christ still matters in the bedroom.
Love still matters.
Gentleness still matters.
Patience still matters.
Honor still matters.
Self-control still matters.
Sacrificial care still matters.
The fruit of the Spirit does not disappear when the bedroom door closes.
And perhaps someone reading this feels an uncomfortable knot forming in the stomach right now.
Because this is no longer theoretical.
Maybe you have been the spouse who pressured.
Maybe you have used sulking, anger, guilt, Scripture, silence, threats, spiritual language, or emotional withdrawal to get your way.
Maybe you never physically forced anything, so you convinced yourself everything was fine.
But somewhere inside, you know.
You were not asking:
“How can I love you?”
You were asking:
“How can I make you give me what I want?”
If that is you, do not defend yourself.
Repent.
Not because sexual desire within marriage is dirty.
It isn't.

Scripture can speak beautifully and positively about marital desire and delight. Proverbs 5:18–19 celebrates marital affection. Song of Songs does not blush at the joy of husband and wife desiring one another. Hebrews 13:4 honors marriage and the marriage bed.
Sex is not the villain.
Selfishness is.
Lust that reduces another person to something consumed is.
Pride is.
Control is.
Manipulation is.
Using God's Word to sanctify our selfishness is.
And repentance does not begin with explaining why your spouse made you behave that way.
Repentance begins when excuses finally die.
“Jesus, I sinned.”
Four words.
No footnotes.
No blame shifting.
No “but she…”
No “but he…”
No “you don't understand how long…”
Just truth.
“Jesus, I sinned.”
And perhaps you are reading from the other side.
You were the one pressured.
The one who learned to freeze.
The one who dreaded bedtime.
The one who felt guilty for having emotions, exhaustion, physical pain, fear, trauma, or limitations.
Maybe someone repeatedly quoted 1 Corinthians 7 until you began associating the voice of God with coercion.
Hear this carefully:
Jesus is not the person who weaponized His Word against you.
Do not confuse the misuse of Scripture with the character of its Author.
Christ is not cruel.
Christ does not need manipulation to establish His authority.
He is “meek and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29).
He sees people others overlook.
He receives the wounded.
He confronts sin without exploiting sinners.
He tells the truth without becoming abusive.
And at the cross, Jesus demonstrates what holy authority actually looks like.
He possesses all authority…
and gives Himself.
That is the scandal at the center of Christianity.
The King bleeds.
The Holy One bears shame.
The innocent Christ receives the judgment sinners deserve.
Jesus does not merely tell broken humanity to become better.
He comes for us.
He carries our sin.
He dies.
He rises.
He calls us to repent and believe.
And then grace begins rewriting people who thought their worst chapters had already determined their ending.
That includes marriages.
Maybe yours is cold right now.
Maybe resentment has accumulated so quietly that you no longer remember when tenderness disappeared.
Maybe sex has become mechanical.
Maybe rejection has created bitterness.
Maybe pornography has poisoned expectations.
Maybe betrayal shattered trust.
Maybe childbirth changed everything.
Maybe illness changed everything.
Maybe age changed everything.
Maybe trauma followed one of you into marriage.
Maybe one spouse feels constantly unwanted while the other feels constantly pressured.
Those wounds will not be healed by ripping one sentence out of 1 Corinthians 7 and throwing it across the bed.
You need truth.
You need difficult conversations.
You may need wise pastoral care.
In serious situations, you may need qualified professional help.

And where coercion, threats, violence, or abuse are present, the answer is not to tell the harmed spouse to endure danger silently because “marriage is sacred.” Seeking safety and appropriate help is not the same thing as despising marriage.
Marriage is sacred.
That is precisely why evil inside marriage should not be baptized with Christian vocabulary.
The goal is not merely more sex.
The goal is a marriage increasingly submitted to Jesus Christ.
Because you can share a bed and still be miles apart.
You can touch someone's body without knowing their heart.
You can technically fulfill a marital obligation while starving your marriage of tenderness.
And you can win an argument about 1 Corinthians 7 while losing the person lying beside you.
Your spouse is not pornography with a wedding ring.
Your spouse is not a mechanism God provided to regulate your sexual appetite.
Your spouse is not a reward for good Christian behavior.
Your spouse is not property.
Your spouse is a person bearing the image of God.
A soul.
A story.
A human being with fears you may not completely understand.
A person with wounds you may not see.
A person who may sometimes need affection that does not become a demand for sex.
A person who may need to know that your kindness is still real when the answer is not what you hoped for.
And yes, your spouse may also be someone quietly aching because rejection has become chronic and unexplained.
Someone wondering whether they are still desirable.
Someone embarrassed to admit how deeply repeated rejection hurts.
Someone who has stopped initiating because another “no” feels unbearable.
That pain matters too.
1 Corinthians 7 should not be weaponized in either direction.
Paul does not provide permission for coercive entitlement.
Neither does he celebrate selfish withholding.
He calls husband and wife away from isolated self-rule and toward reciprocal marital faithfulness.
That means mature Christian couples must learn something far more difficult than quoting verses at one another.
They must learn to talk.
To listen.
To confess.
To forgive.
To understand.
To wait.
To initiate without demanding.
To decline without humiliating.
To express desire without turning desire into entitlement.
To hear pain without immediately becoming defensive.
To address persistent sexual disconnection rather than pretending it does not matter.
To pursue healing where wounds have made intimacy frightening.
To refuse pornography's counterfeit education in sexuality.
To remember that the person beside them is someone Christ commands them to love.
And perhaps the most important question tonight is not:
“Am I getting enough?”
Maybe it is:
“Does my spouse experience the character of Jesus in the way I love them?”
That question is harder.
Because it reaches beyond the bedroom.
How do you speak when you are angry?
What happens when you do not get what you want?
Do you punish?
Withdraw?
Manipulate?
Shame?
Threaten?
Mock?
Compare?
Keep score?
Or can your spouse disagree with you and remain emotionally safe in your presence?
Can they tell you something painful without immediately paying a price for their honesty?
Can you repent without defending your reputation?
Can you forgive without storing ammunition for the next argument?
Can you love when love costs something?
Because Christian marriage is not ultimately about proving who has authority over whose body.
It is about two redeemed sinners learning that they both belong to Christ.
Paul has already established that larger reality earlier in the letter:
“Ye are not your own… For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body.” — 1 Corinthians 6:19–20
Before your body is a bargaining chip in marriage, your entire life belongs to Jesus.
That changes sexuality.
That changes marriage.
That changes the question.
Not:
“How much can I demand?”
But:
“Jesus, how can my sexuality glorify You?”
Not:
“How can I use this verse against my spouse?”
But:
“Lord, what is this verse exposing in me?”
Maybe what it exposes is entitlement.
Maybe resentment.
Maybe fear.
Maybe sexual selfishness.
Maybe deliberate withholding.
Maybe pornography.
Maybe years of unresolved hurt.
Maybe pride.
Maybe shame.
Maybe the inability to say, “I was wrong.”
Whatever Jesus exposes, bring it into the light.
Grace does not mean pretending sin is harmless.
Grace means sinners can finally stop hiding because Christ has made forgiveness possible.
At Calvary, Jesus carried real guilt.
Not imaginary guilt.
Real sin.
Our sin.
And the resurrection announces that sin does not get the final word over those who belong to Him.
So if you have sinned sexually against your spouse, repentance is possible.
If selfishness has corrupted intimacy, repentance is possible.
If bitterness has hardened you, repentance is possible.
If pornography has distorted your understanding of bodies and desire, repentance is possible.
If you have been living behind excuses, repentance is possible.
And if someone else's sin wounded you, their sin does not get to become your identity.
There is grace.
There is truth.
There is a Savior.
His name is Jesus.
Sometimes three words are enough to stop hiding.
Not because every Christian marriage is secretly broken.
Because one day, after an argument, when emotions are louder than wisdom, you may need to read it again and remember:
Your spouse is not the enemy.
Your spouse is not an object.
And Scripture is not your weapon.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with earning God's favor.
You cannot purchase grace.
You cannot share enough Christian posts to erase one sin.
Only Jesus saves.
Only His blood atones.
Only His righteousness can cover the guilty.
We support Gospel work because we have been loved by Christ, not because supporting Gospel work makes Christ love us.
So tonight, before reaching for another verse to prove what your spouse owes you, perhaps put the weapon down.
Look at the person beside you.
Really look.
That is not an object.
That is not an entitlement.
That is not a body placed on earth merely to satisfy you.
That is a human soul.
And if you belong to Jesus, you have been called to love that soul in a way that increasingly resembles the Savior who loved you when you had nothing to offer Him.
Maybe your marriage has chapters you wish had never been written.
Maybe there has been selfishness.
Rejection.
Pressure.
Silence.
Shame.
Sin.
Tears nobody saw.
Nights you cannot get back.
Words you desperately wish you could pull out of the past.
But the Gospel was made for people with chapters they cannot rewrite themselves.
Bring the truth into the light.
Repent where you have sinned.
Seek forgiveness where you have wounded.
Seek help where there is danger or deep brokenness.
Learn to listen.
Learn to honor.
Learn to serve.
Learn to love.
And let Jesus begin writing something neither of you could manufacture alone.
Because perhaps the most intimate thing you can give your spouse is not your body.
Perhaps it is a heart so surrendered to Christ that they no longer have to fear what you will do when you do not get your way.
Remember this:
The hands that should hold your spouse most tenderly are the hands that have finally surrendered their weapons at the feet of Jesus.
